blocks.text:
New Year's Eve takes place on Copacabana. People gather by the water dressed in white, bringing flowers and small offerings to Iemanjá. After the countdown, fireworks begin over the ocean. Before and after the celebration, you will see Rio from Corcovado and Sugarloaf Mountain, then travel to Iguazu. The Brazilian side offers a broad panorama of the whole waterfall system, while the Argentinian side takes you almost to the water itself.

The trip is short but packed with experiences. You will remember Rio for its sights and for the way the city prepares for New Year: stages on the beach, white clothing, evening lights and people gradually filling the promenade. Iguazu unfolds very differently. First you hear the roar, then individual cascades appear, until water fills almost your entire view. The strong contrast between these 2 parts of the route makes the journey feel much longer than a calendar week.

New Year in Rio begins with anticipation. The day before the celebration, Copacabana still looks familiar: a seafront promenade, beach cafés, music, runners and surfers. But hour by hour, more stages, barriers, groups dressed in white, flower sellers and festive activity appear. By the evening of 31 December, the shore has become the city's main gathering place. The ocean is still beside you, but the familiar beach has turned into a vast space where everyone welcomes the New Year together.

The tradition of offerings to Iemanjá adds another dimension to the celebration. Flowers, candles and small baskets are sent out onto the water before midnight. For some, this is a religious act; for others, it is part of local culture and a beautiful New Year custom. Attention then turns to the horizon: the fireworks platforms stand out in the ocean, so the lights rise directly above the water and reflect on its dark surface.

Corcovado and Sugarloaf Mountain are scheduled on either side of the celebration. Before New Year's Eve, you go up to Christ the Redeemer and look down over Rio while the city is still preparing. On 1 January, a different ascent reveals the bays and ocean after the main night. This helps you see how strongly geography shapes Rio: mountains divide the city into districts, beaches stretch along the water, and bays and granite peaks keep appearing between the neighbourhoods.

At Iguazu, the impression builds gradually. On the Brazilian side, you first see separate white ribbons among the greenery, before the full line of cascades opens up. The Argentinian side has a series of trails: paths run above the cascades, below them and finally out to the Devil's Throat. Spending 2 days by the falls therefore gives you very different viewpoints and time to move between them without rushing.
